analysis.one_liner: Delays a rule extending overtime pay to millions of salaried workers by six months.
analysis.headline: The House passed the overtime-delay bill 246-177 on September 28, 2016, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: In May 2016 the Labor Department issued a rule raising the salary cutoff below which salaried workers must be paid time-and-a-half for overtime, extending overtime protection to workers earning between roughly $23,660 and $47,476 a year. This bill would push the rule's start date from December 1, 2016 to June 1, 2017 [S2][S3]. The House passed it almost entirely on party lines; the Senate read it and placed it on its calendar but never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended [S6][S7].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who pay salaried workers below the new cutoff — retailers, restaurant chains, banks, schools, universities, and nonprofits — would get six more months before having to either raise those salaries above roughly $47,476 or pay them overtime.

how_it_helps.text: Postpones the effective date of the Labor Department's overtime rule from December 1, 2016 to June 1, 2017, so employers would not have to comply until June [S2][S3][S4].
States that nothing in the bill authorizes the rule or any part of it beyond what existing law already provides, a signal the delay could be a step toward stopping the rule entirely [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Salaried workers earning between about $23,660 and $47,476 a year — many in retail management, banking, higher education, and nonprofits — would wait another six months for overtime pay, and some could lose the raise employers might otherwise make to avoid paying overtime.
analysis.who_pays_short: Salaried workers earning under the new cutoff

drawbacks.text: Workers just under the new cutoff would go at least six more months without legally required overtime pay, in some cases at wages low enough that extra hours mean real hardship.

Schools, universities, and nonprofits argued the rule would have raised their labor costs sharply within a tight budget window, forcing cuts to services or benefits — the objection this bill responded to.
A delay this narrow and targeted invited the criticism that it was a specific-interest favor rather than a broad regulatory-review bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls on a specific group of low- and mid-paid salaried workers who would have begun receiving overtime pay within weeks; the benefit goes to their employers' labor budgets. There is no compensating gain for workers in the bill — the only stated purpose is postponement, and its rule-of-construction clause pointedly disclaims any endorsement of the rule itself.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 246-177 in late September 2016, but the Senate just placed it on its calendar and never voted, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S6][S7].

narrative.text: The House Committee on Education and the Workforce never took up the bill; instead, leadership brought it straight to the floor under a rule providing one hour of debate [S6].
The House passed it 246-177, with 241 of 245 Republicans voting yes and only 5 of 186 Democrats doing so [S7].
The Senate received the bill on September 29, 2016, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Calendar as No. 662 on November 15, 2016 — after the election — but no vote ever came [S6].
The bill expired with the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017 [S1][S6].

The delay became moot on its own terms: days before the rule's December 1 effective date, a federal judge in Texas blocked it nationwide, and the incoming administration later replaced it in 2019 with a lower threshold of about $35,568 — so employers avoided the rule either way, without the bill passing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of low-paid salaried workers. The bill died, but a court injunction and the change of administration meant the overtime rule never took effect as written, so the bill's intended beneficiaries got the same result without needing it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, by court order and administration change

for.name: Rep. Tim Walberg
for.role: House sponsor (Education and the Workforce Committee)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered its floor introduction remarks [S5][S6].

for.name: House Republican leadership
for.role: Scheduled the bill under a rule rather than through committee
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor with one hour of debate and a closed amendment process via H. Res. 897 [S6].

against.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
against.role: Ranking Member, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Demanded a recorded vote on passage, postponing the result [S6].

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: The Senate never scheduled a vote; the bill sat on the calendar from November 15, 2016 until the Congress ended [S6].

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost exactly by party: 241 of 245 Republicans voted yes, while only 5 of 186 Democrats did, with 177 voting no [S7].

industries.industry: Retailers, restaurant chains, and other employers of salaried staff under $47,476
industries.note: The rule would have required them to raise those salaries or pay overtime; the delay saves six months of that cost, which comes directly out of what affected workers would have earned [S2][S3].

They employ many low-paid salaried staff — postdocs, entry-level administrators, advisers — who would have become newly eligible for overtime. The delay protects their budgets, at the cost of overtime pay for those employees [S2][S4].

The bill is named for them and would spare their budgets a compliance deadline during a funding cycle, but many nonprofit workers earning under the threshold are exactly the workers the rule would pay extra [S4].
